title: Randomization Unit: Users vs Sessions
description: A product team wants to test a redesigned onboarding flow. They are debating whether to randomize at the user level or the session level, since a single user may open multiple sessions during the experiment. Which randomization unit is more appropriate, and what is the primary reason?
options: User level, because it prevents the same person from experiencing both variants and contaminating the effect estimate
Session level, because it generates more data points and shortens the experiment duration
Session level, because session IDs are easier to track in the analytics pipeline
User level, because it guarantees perfectly balanced group sizes
explanation: User-level randomization is more appropriate because if the same person experiences both control and treatment in different sessions, the independence assumption breaks down, diluting or distorting the measured effect. Session-level randomization inflates the apparent sample count but creates within-user interference. Generating more data points (option A) does not help if the data is structurally invalid. Ease of tracking (option C) is an engineering concern that does not affect causal validity. Balanced group sizes (option D) are not guaranteed by user-level assignment and are not the primary motivation for choosing it.
hints: Think about what happens when the same person is exposed to both variants across different sessions.

title: Choosing a Primary Metric
scenario_context: A team is launching an A/B test on a new recommendation widget. They have access to click-through rate (CTR), time spent on page, downstream purchase rate, and number of page scrolls. They want a primary metric that most directly reflects whether the widget is creating genuine value for users.
description: Which metric is the strongest choice?
options: Number of page scrolls, because it reflects deeper engagement with content
Time spent on page, because more time indicates users find the content interesting
Downstream purchase rate, because it most directly captures whether the recommendation led to real user value
Click-through rate on the widget, because it is the most immediate signal of whether users noticed it
explanation: Downstream purchase rate most directly captures genuine value creation — a user completing a purchase demonstrates the recommendation fulfilled a real intent. CTR (option D) measures attention but not value; users may click out of curiosity and leave disappointed. Time on page (option B) can increase due to confusion rather than interest, making it a noisy proxy. Page scrolls (option A) measure behavior even further removed from value and are easy to inflate artificially. A good primary metric should be sensitive, directional, and tied to the outcome the business cares about.
hints: Which metric captures the end outcome the team actually cares about, rather than an intermediate behavior?

title: Null vs Alternative Hypothesis
description: Before launching an experiment to test whether a faster search results page increases query submission rate, a data scientist must specify hypotheses. Which of the following correctly frames the null and alternative hypotheses for this test?
options: Null: the faster page increases query submission rate. Alternative: it has no effect.
Null: the faster page has no effect on query submission rate. Alternative: the faster page increases query submission rate.
Null: the faster page reduces query submission rate. Alternative: it has no effect.
Null: query submission rate is unmeasurable. Alternative: it can be measured after the experiment.
explanation: The null hypothesis is always the default assumption of no effect — that the intervention makes no difference. The alternative hypothesis is the claim the team is trying to find evidence for, which here is that the faster page increases query submission rate. Option A reverses this framing, placing the desired effect in the null, which is logically backward — you cannot 'accept' the null as proven. Options C and D misrepresent what the hypotheses are supposed to assert about the intervention's effect.
hints: The null hypothesis always represents the baseline assumption of 'no change'.

title: What a p-Value Actually Tells You
description: An experiment yields a p-value of 0.03 at a significance threshold of 0.05. A junior analyst says this means there is a 97% probability that the treatment effect is real. A senior analyst disagrees. Which interpretation of the p-value is correct?
options: The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what was collected, if the null hypothesis were true
The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the observed data
The p-value is the probability that the experiment was conducted correctly
The p-value is the probability that the alternative hypothesis is false
explanation: The p-value measures how surprising the observed data would be if the null hypothesis were true. A p-value of 0.03 means that if there were truly no effect, there is only a 3% chance of seeing a result this extreme or more extreme by chance alone. It does not quantify the probability that the null is true (option A), nor does it validate experimental procedure (option C). The junior analyst's '97% probability the effect is real' is a common misinterpretation — the p-value says nothing directly about the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true or false.
hints: The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true — it is a conditional probability.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Type I Error in Practice
description: A team runs an A/B test on a notification feature and sets their significance threshold (alpha) at 0.05. They observe a statistically significant result and ship the feature. Six weeks later, they find no improvement in the long-term metric. Which type of error most likely occurred, and what does it mean?
options: Type II error — they failed to detect a real effect that existed
Type I error — they concluded there was an effect when there was actually none
Type I error — they set alpha too low, missing true positives
Type II error — their sample size was too large, inflating false negatives
explanation: A Type I error (false positive) occurs when the team rejects the null hypothesis even though no true effect exists — they concluded the feature worked when it did not. This is the most likely scenario here: the initial result was a false positive, possibly due to random noise at a 5% alpha threshold. Type II errors (options A and D) are false negatives — failing to detect a real effect — which is the opposite situation. Option C mischaracterizes Type I errors; a lower alpha makes false positives less likely, not more.
hints: Consider which error involves acting on a result that turns out not to be real.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Type II Error and Underpowered Tests
description: A team tests a small UI tweak and finds a p-value of 0.12, so they conclude the feature has no effect and do not ship it. A later deep-dive reveals the feature did improve the metric by 1.5%, a difference that mattered to the business. What error did the team most likely make, and what was its root cause?
options: Type I error, caused by setting alpha too high
Type I error, caused by not correcting for multiple comparisons
Type II error, caused by setting alpha too low, making the test too conservative
Type II error, caused by insufficient statistical power to detect the true effect
explanation: A Type II error (false negative) occurs when the team fails to reject the null hypothesis even though a real effect exists. This is caused by insufficient statistical power — the experiment did not have enough participants or observations to reliably detect the 1.5% improvement. Option A is incorrect because a Type I error means concluding there is an effect when there is none. Option B (multiple comparisons correction) is unrelated to a single-metric test with one result. Option C confuses Type II errors with alpha level; a lower alpha makes the test harder to pass but does not cause false negatives by itself — low power does.
hints: A false negative means you missed a real effect — think about what determines whether an experiment can detect small effects.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Statistical Power Definition
description: A data scientist says that an experiment has 80% power at the planned sample size. A non-technical stakeholder asks what that means. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: If a true effect of the specified size exists, the experiment has an 80% probability of detecting it
There is an 80% chance the experiment will produce a statistically significant result regardless of whether the effect is real
The experiment will produce a result within 80% of the true effect size
80% of the sample will be allocated to the treatment group
explanation: Statistical power is the probability of correctly detecting a true effect when one exists — it is the complement of the Type II error rate. If power is 80% and the effect is real, the experiment has an 80% chance of producing a statistically significant result. Option B is incorrect because power is conditional on a real effect existing, not a blanket probability of significance. Option C describes precision, not power. Option D describes randomization allocation, which has nothing to do with power.
hints: Power is about your ability to detect something that is genuinely there.

title: Factors That Increase Required Sample Size
description: A team is planning an experiment and consults a sample size calculator. They want to know which combination of choices will require the largest sample size. Assume all else equal when comparing each factor.
options: Low baseline conversion rate, small minimum detectable effect, high statistical power
High baseline conversion rate, large minimum detectable effect, high statistical power
High baseline conversion rate, small minimum detectable effect, low statistical power
Low baseline conversion rate, large minimum detectable effect, low statistical power
explanation: Sample size requirements grow when: (1) the minimum detectable effect is small — detecting a tiny signal requires far more observations; (2) desired power is high — fewer missed effects means more data. These are the two dominant drivers. For conversion rates, baseline variance (p × (1 − p)) also plays a role, peaking near 50% — but a low baseline means lower variance, which actually slightly reduces sample demand. In option B, the low baseline works against the conclusion, but the small MDE more than compensates: halving the MDE roughly quadruples required sample. Option B has a large MDE, which slashes the sample requirement despite high baseline variance. Option C has low power, which reduces sample needs at the cost of more false negatives. Option D combines a large MDE and low power, both of which shrink requirements.
hints: Think about how hard it is to distinguish a tiny difference from random noise.
Focus on which two levers dominate sample size and pick the option that pushes both in the most demanding direction.

title: Interpreting a Confidence Interval
description: An experiment on a new pricing page yields a 95% confidence interval for the lift in conversion rate of [+0.2%, +1.8%]. A stakeholder says this means there is a 95% probability that the true effect is between 0.2% and 1.8%. Is the stakeholder correct, and why?
options: Yes — by definition, a 95% confidence interval contains the true parameter with 95% probability
No — the true parameter is fixed; the 95% refers to the procedure: 95% of such intervals constructed from repeated samples would contain the true value
No — the confidence interval only tells us that the null hypothesis can be rejected at alpha = 0.05
Yes — the interval is centered on the sample estimate, which is the most probable true value
explanation: The stakeholder's statement is a common misinterpretation. The true parameter is a fixed (though unknown) value — it either is or is not in any given interval. The 95% confidence level is a property of the procedure: if the experiment were repeated many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter. Option A restates the misconception. Option C is partially true as a corollary — if zero is outside the interval, the result is significant at alpha = 0.05 — but that is not the primary meaning of a confidence interval. Option D is also wrong because the center is just the point estimate, not inherently 'most probable' in a frequentist framework.
hints: Think about whether a single computed interval can have a probability — or whether probability applies to the long-run process of constructing such intervals.

title: One-Sided vs Two-Sided Tests
description: A team is testing a new feed-ranking algorithm. They believe the new algorithm can only improve or stay neutral — it cannot harm engagement. A colleague suggests using a one-sided test. What is the main trade-off of this choice compared to a two-sided test?
options: A one-sided test requires a larger sample size to achieve the same power
A one-sided test is more powerful at detecting an effect in the predicted direction but will not flag harm if the metric moves the other way
A one-sided test is always preferred because it halves the p-value, making results easier to achieve
A one-sided test removes the need for a significance threshold entirely
explanation: A one-sided test concentrates all the statistical power in the predicted direction, making it easier to detect an improvement — but this comes at the cost of completely missing harm if the metric moves in the opposite direction. This is a real risk: 'cannot harm' is often an assumption, not a guarantee. Option A is incorrect; one-sided tests actually require smaller samples than two-sided tests for the same power in one direction. Option C is dangerous reasoning — choosing a one-sided test purely to halve the p-value is p-hacking if the direction wasn't committed to in advance. Option D is wrong; significance thresholds still apply.
hints: What happens to your ability to detect a bad outcome if you only look for improvements?

title: The Role of a Control Group
description: A team launches a new feature to all users and measures whether session length increased compared to the prior week. A data scientist raises a concern about this approach. What is the most important problem with running the experiment this way?
options: Session length is not a valid metric for measuring feature success
The experiment should have been run for longer than one week
They should have measured daily active users instead of session length
There is no concurrent control group, so any change in session length could be caused by factors other than the feature
explanation: Without a concurrent control group, it is impossible to isolate the feature's effect from other simultaneous changes — seasonality, external events, product changes, or traffic mix shifts could all explain the observed difference. This is a confounding problem, not a metric problem. Option A is wrong because session length is a reasonable engagement metric. Option B may or may not be true but is secondary to the structural flaw of having no control. Option C is a metric preference and does not address the causal identification problem.
hints: Without a comparison group running at the same time, how do you know what caused the change?

title: Unexpected Traffic Imbalance at Experiment Start
scenario_context: A team launches a 50/50 A/B test on a new onboarding flow. After two days, they check the assignment counts: control has 5,800 users and treatment has 4,200 users. The assignment code was supposed to split traffic equally.
description: What should the team do first?
options: Investigate whether the assignment mechanism is working correctly before reading any results
Proceed with analysis — a 58/42 split is close enough to 50/50 for practical purposes
Extend the experiment until the treatment group catches up in size
Reweight the treatment group observations to match the control group size, then analyze
explanation: A meaningful imbalance in traffic allocation signals that the randomization or assignment pipeline may be broken — users may not be independently assigned, certain segments may be excluded from one arm, or a logging error may have under-counted treatment exposures. Before reading any metric, the team must understand why the split is off. Acting on results from a broken experiment risks acting on a biased estimate whose direction and magnitude are unknown. Option B is wrong: a 38-percentage-point gap from expected is not noise — it warrants investigation. Option C extends a potentially broken experiment, producing more contaminated data, not better data. Option D applies a post-hoc correction that cannot fix a structural assignment bias.
hints: If the traffic split is not what you designed, what does that tell you about the experiment's infrastructure before you look at any metric?

title: Peeking at Results Early
scenario_context: A team launches an A/B test and plans to run it for four weeks. At the end of week one, results look promising with p = 0.04. A stakeholder wants to stop the experiment early and ship the feature.
description: What is the primary risk of stopping now?
options: The sample size is large enough at week one, so there is no statistical risk
Stopping early guarantees a Type II error because the effect estimate will be too small
Stopping early because the result looks significant inflates the Type I error rate beyond the planned alpha
There is no risk as long as the team re-runs the full experiment afterward
explanation: Stopping an experiment early when results look significant — often called 'peeking' — inflates the false positive rate well above the stated alpha. This is because by checking repeatedly, you give random fluctuations more chances to cross the significance threshold. The planned experiment had an alpha of 0.05 over four weeks, but the actual false positive risk is higher when using an early stopping rule not accounted for in the design. Option A is wrong; sample size and statistical validity are not the same thing. Option B confuses early stopping with Type II errors — early stopping biases toward finding significance, not missing it. Option D is incorrect because re-running is not a valid post-hoc correction.
hints: Think about how many opportunities the team is giving random noise to look like a real signal.

title: Guardrail Metrics
description: A team runs an A/B test on a new ad placement and observes that their primary metric (ad revenue per user) significantly increases in the treatment group. However, they also notice that average session length drops by 8% in treatment. How should the team interpret this finding?
options: The experiment is a success because the primary metric improved significantly
The drop in session length is expected for ad experiments and can be ignored
Session length is irrelevant because it was not pre-specified as the primary metric
The result is mixed — the primary metric improved, but a guardrail metric suggests user experience may be degrading
explanation: Guardrail metrics exist to detect harm that primary metrics might miss. A significant drop in session length suggests users are leaving earlier, possibly due to ad intrusiveness — this is a meaningful signal even if revenue per user went up. Shipping the feature ignores the possibility of long-term user attrition. Option A is dangerously narrow; optimizing one metric while harming another can destroy long-term value. Option B is an unfounded assumption — the drop should be investigated, not dismissed. Option C is incorrect; pre-specified guardrail metrics are standard practice precisely because they are not the primary metric but still matter.
hints: Think about whether a win on one metric can still represent an overall loss for the product.

title: Selecting a Sensitive Metric
description: A team is testing a new search ranking model and must choose a primary metric. They are considering: (A) 30-day user retention, (B) daily active users, (C) mean reciprocal rank of the first clicked result, or (D) quarterly revenue. Which metric is most likely to be sensitive enough to detect a ranking improvement in a two-week experiment?
options: 30-day user retention, because it captures the full downstream effect on loyalty
Quarterly revenue, because revenue is the ultimate business outcome
Daily active users, because it is a well-understood and widely tracked metric
Mean reciprocal rank of the first clicked result, because it directly reflects search quality and responds quickly
explanation: Mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of the first clicked result is a behavioral signal that changes immediately as users interact with the new ranking — it is tightly coupled to the intervention and responds within the two-week window. Retention (option A) and quarterly revenue (option B) are lagging indicators that take weeks or months to reflect ranking quality changes, making them insensitive for short experiments. Daily active users (option C) is a coarse metric that aggregates far too many factors to be sensitive to a ranking change in two weeks.
hints: Choose the metric most directly affected by what the experiment actually changes.

title: Confidence Interval and Practical Significance
description: An experiment on a checkout redesign yields a 95% confidence interval for conversion rate lift of [+0.01%, +0.05%]. The result is statistically significant. The engineering cost to ship the feature is six weeks of work. How should the team interpret this result?
options: Ship immediately — statistical significance proves the feature is worth building
Discard the result — confidence intervals above zero are not meaningful
Investigate whether the lift is large enough to justify the cost, since statistical significance does not imply practical significance
Increase the sample size to widen the confidence interval before deciding
explanation: Statistical significance tells you the effect is unlikely to be zero, but it says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter. A lift of 0.01–0.05% in conversion rate may be genuine but far too small to justify six weeks of engineering effort. The team must compare the expected business impact to the cost. Option A conflates statistical and practical significance, a very common error. Option B is wrong; narrow, positive intervals are valid and informative. Option D misunderstands the direction: more sample narrows a confidence interval, not widens it. Even if the team were to narrow the interval further, a tight interval around a 0.01–0.05% lift still reveals a tiny effect — it does not change the practical significance problem.
hints: Ask: even if this effect is real, is it large enough to be worth acting on?

title: Experiment Duration and Day-of-Week Effects
description: A team launches an A/B test on a Monday and, after collecting two days of data, observes a significant lift. They consider ending the experiment. A colleague warns against this. What is the most likely concern the colleague is raising?
options: Two days is always too short because regulatory compliance requires longer experiments
The team should only end experiments on Fridays to avoid data pipeline issues
The early results may reflect Monday–Tuesday user behavior only, which may not be representative of the full weekly cycle
Two days of data always means an underpowered test regardless of traffic volume
explanation: User behavior varies significantly by day of the week — weekday users often behave differently from weekend users. Ending an experiment after only two weekdays means the results are drawn from a non-representative slice of the weekly cycle, which can produce misleading lift estimates. This is a day-of-week confound, not a sample size issue. Option A introduces a regulatory constraint that does not apply here. Option B is logistical superstition, not a statistical principle. Option D is incorrect; two days of high-traffic data can be adequately powered — the problem is representativeness, not power.
hints: Think about whether users on Monday and Tuesday behave the same as users throughout the entire week.

title: A/A Test Purpose
description: Before running a major product experiment, a data scientist recommends running an A/A test — splitting users into two identical experiences with no actual treatment difference. The engineering team questions the value of this. What is the primary purpose of an A/A test?
options: To measure the baseline metric before the real experiment begins
To verify that the experimentation infrastructure assigns users randomly and produces expected false positive rates
To train the model used by the experiment's analysis pipeline
To identify which users should be excluded from the real experiment
explanation: An A/A test validates the experimentation platform itself: if two identical groups show a statistically significant difference, it signals a problem with randomization, logging, or the analysis pipeline. Well-functioning platforms should produce significant A/A results roughly at the stated alpha rate (e.g., ~5% of the time at alpha = 0.05). Option A describes what a pre-experiment baseline period does, which is different. Option C is unrelated — A/A tests do not train models. Option D describes an exclusion or eligibility filter, not what an A/A test accomplishes.
hints: If both groups are identical, what would a significant result tell you about your setup?

title: Increasing Power Without More Users
scenario_context: A team has already recruited the maximum number of users they can for an experiment, but their power analysis suggests they are underpowered for the effect size they care about.
description: Which of the following approaches can increase statistical power without acquiring more users?
options: Switch to a two-sided test instead of a one-sided test
Reduce the minimum detectable effect to a smaller number
Raise the significance threshold from 0.05 to 0.10, accepting more false positives to reduce false negatives
Run fewer metrics to simplify the analysis
explanation: Raising alpha (the significance threshold) directly increases power at the cost of a higher false positive rate — this is a genuine trade-off teams sometimes accept when sample sizes are constrained. Every unit of alpha you give up on Type I error buys you a corresponding reduction in Type II error. Option A is wrong; switching from one-sided to two-sided reduces power for the predicted direction. Option B sounds intuitive but is backwards — a smaller minimum detectable effect means you are trying to detect something smaller, which requires more power, not less. Option D has no meaningful effect on statistical power.
hints: Power and the significance threshold are directly linked — moving one affects the other.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Logging at the Step Level in a Checkout Experiment
scenario_context: A team is designing an A/B test on a redesigned checkout flow. They plan to measure whether the new design increases overall purchase completion rate. A data scientist recommends also logging which step each user abandons — payment details, shipping confirmation, or review page.
description: What is the primary benefit of logging at the step level?
options: It enables the team to understand where in the funnel the treatment effect concentrates, which helps diagnose whether a lift is genuine and why it occurred
Step-level logging reduces the variance of the primary metric, making the experiment more powerful
Step-level logging replaces the need for a primary metric because it captures all user behavior
It allows the team to run separate statistical tests on each step without inflating the false positive rate
explanation: Logging where users drop off provides diagnostic depth: if the new checkout design improves completion, step-level data reveals which friction point was resolved — payment entry, shipping confusion, or the review stage. This makes the result actionable and defensible. Without step-level data, a positive result is a black box: you know something worked but not what or why, making it hard to iterate or reproduce. Option B is wrong; logging additional events does not reduce variance in the primary metric. Option C is wrong; granular logging complements, not replaces, a pre-specified primary metric. Option D is incorrect: logging additional events does not resolve multiple-testing inflation — analyzing each step as a separate significance test would still inflate Type I error.
hints: If the overall metric improves, what additional information would help you understand why and where?

title: Feature Only Visible to a Subset of Assigned Users
scenario_context: A team wants to test a new in-app notification badge that only appears in the mobile app. They randomly assign 50% of all users — mobile and desktop — to the treatment group. Desktop users assigned to treatment see no badge and have an identical experience to control.
description: What is the primary problem with this experiment design?
options: Randomizing at the user level is incorrect for notification features — session-level randomization is required
The experiment should only launch when at least 80% of the user base is on mobile to ensure adequate power
Desktop users assigned to treatment receive no exposure to the feature, diluting the measured effect and reducing the experiment's sensitivity
Including non-mobile users inflates the false positive rate by introducing uncontrolled variance from a non-target segment
explanation: Desktop users assigned to treatment contribute zero signal — they never saw the badge, so their outcomes are identical to control users. Including them in the treatment arm inflates the denominator without adding useful data, which dilutes the estimated effect toward zero and reduces the experiment's ability to detect a real impact. The fix is to restrict assignment to mobile users, or to analyze only the triggered population. Option A is wrong: user-level randomization is appropriate here; session-level would allow the same person to land in both groups across sessions. Option B introduces an arbitrary threshold with no statistical justification. Option D mislabels the mechanism: the problem is reduced power through dilution, not inflated Type I error.
hints: If a large share of users assigned to treatment can never actually see the feature, what happens to the measured treatment effect?

title: Carryover Effects When Starting a Follow-On Experiment
description: A team ships a successful feature and immediately launches a new experiment on the same user population. A data scientist warns this could introduce bias. What is the most likely concern?
options: Users cannot be randomized a second time once they have participated in a previous experiment
The statistical power of the new experiment is permanently reduced because the eligible pool is now smaller
Running two experiments in the same calendar quarter violates standard industry experiment-governance rules
Users who experienced the previous treatment may still be behaviorally influenced by it, so their baseline in the new experiment is not clean
explanation: When a treatment is shipped, users who were exposed to it may carry changed behaviors, expectations, or habits into the next experiment. If a new experiment starts immediately, those users are not at a clean behavioral baseline — their responses may still reflect the prior change rather than their natural state. This carryover contamination can bias the new experiment's measured effect in either direction. The standard mitigation is a washout period or restricting the new experiment to users who were not exposed to the prior treatment. Option A is incorrect: users can be re-randomized, but their behavioral baseline may not be independent. Option B is wrong: pool size is not the issue here. Option C invents a governance rule that does not exist.
hints: Think about whether users who just experienced a changed product are behaving the same way they would have before that change.

title: Defining the Minimum Detectable Effect
description: A team is planning a sample size calculation and needs to specify a minimum detectable effect (MDE). A stakeholder asks why they cannot just set the MDE to 0.01% to be maximally sensitive. What is the most important practical consequence of setting an extremely small MDE?
options: A smaller MDE requires a much larger sample size, which may be infeasible given traffic levels and time constraints
A smaller MDE always reduces statistical power, making the test less reliable
A smaller MDE increases the Type I error rate regardless of alpha setting
Setting MDE below 0.1% makes statistical testing mathematically undefined
explanation: The minimum detectable effect and required sample size are inversely related: halving the MDE roughly quadruples the required sample. Setting an extremely small MDE may require millions of users and months of time — resources that are simply not available. This makes the design impractical. Option B is backwards; a smaller MDE does not reduce power — it requires more sample to achieve the same power. Option C is wrong; MDE does not independently affect alpha. Option D is incorrect; there is no mathematical lower bound on MDE, only practical ones.
hints: How does the size of the effect you want to detect relate to how much data you need?

title: High-Variance Metric and Required Sample Size
description: A team wants to measure the impact of a new pricing page on revenue per user. The metric has very high variance: most users spend nothing, but a small number of users make purchases worth hundreds of dollars. What is the most direct consequence of this metric's variance on the experiment?
options: High variance systematically biases the p-value upward, increasing the likelihood of a false positive
The team will need a much larger sample size to detect a real effect because the noise in the metric swamps the expected signal
High variance is only a concern for non-normal distributions and can be ignored if the overall sample is large enough
The team should cap revenue at a maximum value per user, which will eliminate the need for a larger sample
explanation: Statistical power depends on the signal-to-noise ratio. When metric variance is high — driven here by a handful of large purchases — the noise is large relative to the expected treatment effect, and many more observations are needed to reliably distinguish a real signal from random fluctuation. Required sample size scales with metric variance: doubling variance roughly doubles the required n. Option A is wrong: high variance inflates standard errors, which makes results harder to achieve statistical significance (Type II error increases), not easier (Type I error is not affected this way). Option C misapplies the central limit theorem — normality of the sampling distribution is restored by large samples, but high variance still inflates required n regardless of distributional shape. Option D describes a real variance-reduction technique, but it is a mitigation strategy, not a consequence of high variance.
hints: If the metric bounces widely from user to user, how much data does an experiment need to reliably detect the difference between two groups?

title: Predicting CI Width After Quadrupling Sample Size
description: An experiment with 10,000 users produces a 95% confidence interval for conversion rate lift of [−0.5%, +2.1%], with a point estimate of +0.8%. The team reruns the experiment with 40,000 users under identical conditions. Assuming the true effect is unchanged, which of the following best describes the expected new confidence interval?
options: The confidence interval narrows to roughly half its original width, and the point estimate remains close to +0.8%, giving an interval near [+0.15%, +1.45%]
The confidence interval width stays the same — more data improves accuracy of the point estimate but not the interval width
The confidence interval widens because a larger sample surfaces more variability in user behavior
The confidence interval collapses to a single point equal to the true effect because 40,000 users is a sufficiently large sample
explanation: Confidence interval width is inversely proportional to the square root of sample size. Quadrupling the sample (10,000 → 40,000) halves the standard error (√4 = 2), which halves the interval width. The original half-width is 1.3 percentage points ([−0.5%, +2.1%] spans 2.6pp, so ±1.3pp). After quadrupling, the expected half-width is approximately ±0.65pp, giving a new interval of roughly [+0.15%, +1.45%]. The point estimate remains near +0.8% because the true effect has not changed. Option B is wrong: width is a function of standard error, which does shrink with more data. Option C is wrong: larger samples reduce sampling variability, not increase it. Option D is wrong: no finite sample collapses the interval to a point — increasing n narrows the interval but cannot eliminate it.
hints: Recall the relationship between confidence interval width and the square root of sample size.

title: Interpreting a Non-Significant Result
description: An experiment on a new feature returns a p-value of 0.18, and the team concludes 'the feature has no effect.' A senior analyst challenges this conclusion. What is the most precise objection the analyst could make?
options: A p-value above 0.05 proves the null hypothesis is true, so the analyst is correct to conclude no effect
Failing to reject the null hypothesis does not prove there is no effect — it may mean the experiment lacked power to detect one
A non-significant result means the experiment failed and should be discarded entirely
The team should re-run the experiment with a higher alpha to obtain a significant result
explanation: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. A p-value of 0.18 means the data are not inconsistent with the null hypothesis — it does not confirm the null is true. The experiment may have been underpowered, making the test unable to detect a real but small effect. The correct language is 'we found no statistically significant evidence of an effect,' not 'there is no effect.' Option A is a logical error; null hypothesis significance testing cannot prove the null. Option C is too strong — a null result is informative and should be documented. Option D is p-hacking and should not be recommended.
hints: Think carefully about what a non-significant result actually proves versus what it fails to disprove.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Defining Experiment Eligibility Criteria
scenario_context: A team is testing a new checkout experience and wants to include all users in the experiment. A data scientist suggests restricting the experiment to users who have at least one item in their cart.
description: What is the strongest reason for this restriction?
options: Users without items in their cart will dilute the treatment group and bias the result toward zero
Including ineligible users violates GDPR and should be avoided for compliance reasons
The experiment platform cannot handle users with empty carts
Users who never reach the checkout have no exposure to the feature, so including them adds noise and reduces sensitivity
explanation: Including users who never reach the checkout page means including many people for whom the treatment effect is mechanically zero — they never saw the new experience. These null-exposure users dilute the measured effect and increase noise without contributing signal, reducing the sensitivity of the test. Restricting to cart-holders focuses the experiment on the population that actually matters for the question being asked. Option A describes a real consequence but uses imprecise language ('bias'); the issue is noise inflation and reduced power, not systematic bias. Option B is not applicable here. Option C is a fictional platform constraint.
hints: If a user never encounters the feature being tested, what is their contribution to the experiment?

title: Confidence Interval Width and Sample Size
description: A team runs a two-week experiment on a new feature and computes a 95% confidence interval for conversion rate lift of [−3%, +4%]. They want a more precise estimate. Which of the following approaches would most reliably narrow the confidence interval?
options: Switch from a 95% confidence level to a 90% confidence level and recompute
Increase the experiment's sample size by running it for a longer period or on more traffic
Remove outlier users from the analysis post-hoc
Change the primary metric to one with a higher absolute value
explanation: Confidence interval width is primarily determined by sample size — more data means a more precise estimate of the true effect. Running the experiment longer or on a larger share of traffic is the most reliable way to narrow the interval. Option A would narrow the interval slightly but by reducing the confidence level — you get a tighter interval only by accepting more uncertainty about whether the true value is inside it. Option C introduces selection bias and can distort the estimate, not just narrow it. Option D changes what is being measured and does not make the estimate of conversion lift more precise.
hints: Think about what drives the width of a confidence interval in terms of data quantity.

title: Pre-Registering Hypotheses
description: Before launching an experiment, a data scientist writes down the primary metric, the expected direction of the effect, and the significance threshold in a shared document. A colleague asks why this step matters. What is the most important reason for pre-registering experiment details before collecting data?
options: Pre-registration is required by the experimentation platform and cannot be skipped
Pre-registration guarantees that the experiment will produce a statistically significant result
Pre-registration allows the team to skip the analysis step if the results match the hypothesis
Pre-registration prevents the team from changing hypotheses, metrics, or thresholds after seeing the data, which would inflate false positive rates
explanation: Pre-registration creates a commitment to a specific analysis plan before the data are collected. Without it, teams may unconsciously (or consciously) change the primary metric, adjust the significance threshold, or switch from two-sided to one-sided tests after seeing results — all of which inflate the true false positive rate beyond the stated alpha. This practice is sometimes called 'HARKing' (hypothesizing after results are known). Option A invents a technical requirement that does not exist. Option B is wrong; pre-registration constrains analysis choices but has no effect on the underlying probability of a true effect. Option C is the opposite of good practice — pre-registration mandates rigorous analysis, not a shortcut past it.
hints: What happens to your claimed false positive rate if you can keep changing your analysis until results look good?

title: Re-Running an Experiment Until Significant
description: An experiment returns p = 0.09, which is not significant at alpha = 0.05. The team reruns the identical experiment with a fresh user sample. The second run returns p = 0.04, and they report a significant positive result. What is the statistical problem with this approach?
options: The second run is statistically valid because it used an independent sample with no overlap from the first run
Running the experiment twice doubles the required sample size, which violates the original power assumptions
Each run independently carries a 5% chance of a false positive, so running twice inflates the cumulative false positive rate to approximately 9.75%, nearly double the stated alpha
The second run is only valid if the first run had at least 80% power to detect the true effect
explanation: Each independent run at alpha = 0.05 carries a 5% chance of producing a false positive when there is no true effect. Running the same hypothesis test twice and reporting a result when either run is significant raises the true false positive rate to 1 − (0.95)² ≈ 9.75% — nearly double the stated alpha. This is the same family-wise error accumulation that occurs when running multiple simultaneous tests. The correct approach is to pre-specify a single run with adequate power, or to use a sequential testing method that controls Type I error across multiple looks. Option A is wrong: an independent sample does not reset the cumulative false positive risk across two testing decisions. Option B is wrong: sample size requirements are unrelated to the inflation problem. Option D introduces an arbitrary power threshold that has no bearing on the validity concern here.
hints: If each test independently has a 5% chance of a false positive, what is the probability of getting at least one false positive across two tests?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS
